n: On Easter Sunday, April 3, 1836, one week after the dedication, Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery prayed behind curtains at the Melchizedek Priesthood pulpits. Spiritual eyes were opened, and they saw beyond the ordinary world.

f.w: The veil was taken from our minds

n: They saw the Lord standing on the front rail of the pulpit. The gold pavement beneath him recalls what Moses and the elders of Israel saw on Sinai.

f.g: The front ledge or railing of the raised pulpit.

f.w: a paved work of pure gold

n: The description closely parallels John’s vision of the risen Christ: flaming eyes, snow-white hair, a face brighter than the sun, a voice like rushing waters. The speaker is Jehovah—Jesus Christ.

f.w: His eyes were as a flame of fire

n: Christ identifies himself as the eternal, living One who was crucified—and as the one who pleads our case before the Father.

f.w: I am the first and the last

n: The first words to Joseph and Oliver are forgiveness and joy. Before keys are given, the Savior assures them they are clean.

f.w: lift up your heads and rejoice

n: The Lord invites all the Saints who sacrificed to build the temple to share in this joy.
Here is the direct answer to the dedicatory prayer: the Lord accepts the house and promises to reveal himself there in mercy.
The Lord promises to appear and speak to his servants—on condition that the people keep his commandments and keep the temple holy.

f.w: do not pollute this holy house

n: Countless people will rejoice because of the blessings and the “endowment” of power the Lord’s servants received in this temple.

f.g: A gift, especially of spiritual power; the Kirtland endowment was a preparatory outpouring before the fuller Nauvoo temple ordinances.

n: The temple’s fame will reach other lands, and this is only “the beginning” of blessings—pointing toward many temples to come.

f.g: Today Latter-day Saints have temples on every inhabited continent.

n: Next Moses appears. As the prophet who led Israel out of Egypt, he gives Joseph and Oliver the keys—the authority to direct—the gathering of scattered Israel, including the lost ten tribes.

f.w: the ten tribes from the land of the north

f.g: The right to direct and authorize the use of priesthood power for a particular work.

n: A messenger called Elias restores the “dispensation of the gospel of Abraham”—the covenant promises made to Abraham, including that through his seed all nations would be blessed.

f.g: Greek form of Elijah, but used in latter-day scripture as a title for a forerunner or restorer; this messenger’s identity is not otherwise specified.

f.w: in us and our seed all generations after us should be blessed

n: Then Elijah appears—the Old Testament prophet who was taken to heaven in a chariot of fire without dying.

f.w: taken to heaven without tasting death

n: Elijah announces that Malachi’s prophecy—that Elijah would come before the great day of the Lord—is now fulfilled. Many Jewish families set a place for Elijah at Passover; this appearance came during the Passover season of 1836.

f.w: spoken of by the mouth of Malachi

n: Elijah’s purpose is to bind families together across generations. Without these sealing ties, the earth would be “smitten with a curse”—God’s purpose for his children would fail.

f.w: turn the hearts of the fathers to the children

n: Elijah hands over the keys for this final dispensation—understood by Latter-day Saints as the sealing power that makes temple ordinances binding in heaven. His coming is a sign that the Second Coming is near.
